//: Copy to ~/.config/adjutant/config.json (or point ADJUTANT_CONFIG at it). Keys under `repos` are `owner/name` as the repository's origin remote reports it. A repo entry holds `taskSources` (an array — one code repo often takes work from several trackers, each with its own issueKey and branch prefix); a single-source repo may use the flat shorthand instead. `issueKey` must be unique within an entry. Anything omitted falls back to `defaults`, then to adjutant's own built-in defaults. `//` keys anywhere in this file are documentation and are stripped before the config reaches a session.
//templates: Every escape hatch below is a command template. Placeholders are substituted ALREADY SHELL-QUOTED, so do not put quotes around them: write -n {title}, not -n '{title}'. Omit a key to get the built-in; set it to false to turn the behaviour off entirely (which is a different answer from omitting it). For anything longer than one command, point at a script ("hubWake": "~/bin/wake.sh {pid} {line}") rather than wrapping it in sh -c '…' — a substituted value brings its own quoting and would end the wrapper's quoted string early.
//terminal: spawn: open a tab. focus: raise one. close: close the one a finished worker is sitting in. attach: open a tmux session in your own terminal (what the board runs to open a session in a terminal). title: name a tab. Used both by a session naming itself (the hub calls `adjutant title` at startup) and by every tab `spawn` opens, whose shell calls the same thing — one setting, every tab. Placeholders: spawn {cwd} {title} {command}, focus {pid} {tty} {title}, close {pid} {tty} {title}, title {title}, attach {socket} {session} {window} — where {pid} and {tty} are the operating system's names for a session, not the terminal's own ids for a pane or a window. A spawn template containing {cwd} is trusted to change directory itself; one without gets a `cd` prepended. Defaults are iTerm2 on macOS (spawn/focus/close) and an OSC escape written to this process's tty for title.

terminal.//preset: Built-in preset backend: "tmux" or omitted (default iTerm2 on macOS). Setting "preset": "tmux" enables first-class tmux integration: detached window spawning (`tmux new-window -d`), automatic PID/TTY-to-pane mapping for wake, focus (`select-window` + `select-pane`), and close (`kill-window`), without any custom wrapper scripts.
terminal.//session: Target tmux session name for workers (default: "adjutant"). Overridden by $ADJUTANT_TMUX_SESSION.
terminal.//socket: Optional tmux socket name (runs tmux with -L <socket>). Overridden by $ADJUTANT_TMUX_SOCKET.
terminal.//spawn: Custom spawn template override: tmux new-window -d -c {cwd} -n {title} {command} | ghostty --working-directory={cwd} -e {command} | wezterm cli spawn --cwd {cwd} -- {command}
terminal.//focus: How to raise a session's tab. {pid} is that session's OS process and {tty} the terminal device it is on (ttys004) — neither one is a terminal's own pane or window id. Point this at a wrapper that does the lookup, e.g. raise-tab {tty}.
terminal.//attach: How the board opens a tmux session in your own terminal. {socket} is the tmux socket arguments (-L name, -S path, or nothing) and is inserted as it is; {session} is a session made for this open, in the same group as the original and already showing {window}, so opening it moves nobody else's window. The command has to return at once (a terminal that stays in the foreground holds the request). Unset, the default is a new iTerm2 window running `tmux -CC attach`, and only on a Mac that has iTerm2; anywhere else the board refuses and names this key. Example: ghostty -e tmux {socket} attach -t {session}
terminal.//close: How to close the tab of a worker whose task is over, used by `adj close`. Point this at a wrapper (close-tab {tty}) or set to false to close no tabs at all.
terminal.//title: A tmux rename, a wrapper of your own, anything: tmux rename-window {title}.

//wake: How to get a RUNNING session's attention once a message has landed in its box. A file appearing in a directory wakes nobody, so this is what closes the loop; it runs only when the session is actually up, and a failure never fails the delivery. Placeholders: {pid} {tty} {subject} {line}. Default: iTerm2 `write text` into the session on that tty, which reaches an interactive agent exactly as if the person had typed it; the line and its Enter go as two writes, because an agent can take the two sent together as a paste and never submit it. A template should do the same. Examples: a wrapper of your own, wake-tab {tty} {line} — {pid} and {tty} are the operating system's names for the session while `tmux -t` and `wezterm --pane-id` want the terminal's own target, so something has to map one to the other and a template that skips that step types into whichever pane held the number. Set it to false to never wake anything.
//hubWake: Overrides `wake` for the hub direction only. The long form {"command": …, "line": …} lets you change one half: `command` is a property of the terminal, `line` is the sentence typed at the woken session and is a property of the AGENT — the built-in names MCP tools (adjutant_pending), which is the wrong instruction for an agent that only has the CLI or one that wants a slash command. Omit `command` to keep the machine's mechanism and change only what is said.
//workerWake: The same for the worker direction. Two directions rather than one because the hub and its workers are not always the same agent: `"agentRunner": "codex exec {prompt}"` with a claude hub is exactly the case where the two need different sentences. Built-in line names adjutant_outbox.
//notification: How to interrupt the human. Placeholders: {title} {message} {nwo} ({nwo} is the repository the message is about, the value --repo takes: owner/name, or the checkout's directory name when it has no usable remote). Default: terminal-notifier if installed, else osascript — a notification osascript posts is credited to Script Editor and clicking it opens an empty Script Editor. No default off macOS: set this or a Linux hub notifies nobody. Examples: notify-send {title} {message} | printf '\a' | curl -s -X POST -d {message} https://hooks.example.invalid/… | ntfy publish mytopic {message}
//defaults: Everything here is inherited by every repo entry, and an entry's own key wins. A task source is the one thing that is NOT inherited: merged into an entry that already declares its own, a default source adds a phantom with no issueRepo behind it. Writing `taskSource` here is ignored and reported in `warnings`.

defaults.//ide: Editor for `adj ide --worktree <path>`. A preset name (code, cursor, idea, subl) or a command template containing {worktree}. No built-in: guessing puts you in the wrong editor, so leaving it out is reported in `warnings` and the prompts ask.
defaults.//baseBranch: What a new worktree branches from. "auto" means the newest `origin/release/*` if the repo has any, otherwise the default branch. A branch name here instead pins it. This is the default, not a constraint: a single dispatch can be told to branch from somewhere else without this key changing.
defaults.//reviewBots: Review accounts whose comments a worker waits for before calling a round done. Exactly as GitHub spells them, `[bot]` suffix included.
defaults.//selfReviewRounds: How many self-review rounds a worker runs before handing over. The cap, not a target: it stops when a round finds nothing.
defaults.//reviewEffort: How hard the review engine is asked to look: low | medium | high | xhigh | max.
defaults.//reviewEngine: Who reviews the diff in each self-review round. "auto" sends it to codex while Claude's 5-hour window is at 50% or more or its 7-day window is above 70% (read from rate-limit-cache.json under the session's config directory, and only when codex is on PATH), and to Claude otherwise; `adj review-engine` gives the answer. "claude" or "codex" pins one.
defaults.//draftPr: Open pull requests as drafts. The worker marks one ready only once its own review rounds have converged.
defaults.//copilotReview: Whether a worker asks Copilot to review the pull request it opens: "ask" asks the person every time, "always" requests the review without asking, "never" neither asks nor requests. Not the same thing as reviewBots, which names the reviews a worker waits for once they have been requested. Any other value is reported in `warnings` and treated as "ask".
defaults.//agentRunner: Command that starts a worker. Default: claude --session-id {sessionId} --permission-mode auto {prompt}. Placeholders: {sessionId} {prompt} {worktree} {title}. {sessionId} is a fresh id saved in the worktree so `adj worker --resume` can reopen this exact session; a template without it starts workers that cannot be resumed. Examples: codex exec {prompt} | agy --dangerously-skip-permissions -i {prompt}
defaults.//agentResumeRunner: Command that reopens a worker's saved session (`adj worker --resume`, `adj work --resume`). Default: claude --resume {sessionId} --permission-mode auto {prompt}. Same placeholders as agentRunner, and {sessionId} is required: without it the agent cannot be told which session to reopen, so --resume refuses to run.
defaults.//hubRunner: Command that starts the hub itself. Default: claude -n {name} --session-id {sessionId} --permission-mode auto {prompt}. Placeholders: {name} {sessionId} {prompt}. The session has to be named — the name is the address a report is sent to — and it starts unattended, because a hub waiting for approval is a hub not reading its inbox and nobody is watching that tab. Drop the mode here if you would rather it asked; you will then want a tool allowlist in the agent's own settings. **Keep {name}**: it is the hub's address, and without it the session is nameless in every listing a person reads. A template without it is reported in `warnings`. {sessionId} is a fresh id saved in the state directory so `adj hub --resume` can reopen this exact session; leave it out and the hub still runs but cannot be resumed. Whether the hub is *running* does not depend on it — that rests on the recorded start time, which `exec` preserves and a recycled pid cannot match.
defaults.//hubResumeRunner: Command that reopens the hub's saved session (`adj hub --resume`). Default: claude -n {name} --resume {sessionId} --permission-mode auto {prompt}. Same placeholders as hubRunner, and {sessionId} is required — a resume that cannot say which session would reopen whatever the agent picks, which in the main checkout is as likely to be unrelated work. Change it together with hubRunner when you drop the permission mode.
defaults.//hubAutoResumeHours: How many hours after a hub ended a plain `adj hub` resumes it instead of starting a new one. Default: 3. 0 turns it off, leaving `adj hub --resume` as the only way back; `adj hub --new` starts fresh inside the window. When the hub ended is written by its MCP server (every minute, and once more as the agent closes it), so with no MCP server under the hub there is no answer and `adj hub` starts fresh. A custom hubRunner also needs a hubResumeRunner for this: the built-in resume command would drop whatever the runner adds, so without one only `--resume` brings the hub back. A number, not a string: anything else is reported in `warnings` and the default is used.
defaults.//startupDashboard: Whether a hub hands the dashboard collection to a subagent as it starts. Default: true. Set it to false and the hub comes up having read nothing but its own settings — no board search, no GraphQL, no PR listing — and says so when it goes to wait. **Only the startup collection is affected**: ask it for the listing and it collects, exactly as before, which is the point of turning the automatic one off rather than the feature. A hub that is scoped to a parent task collects that parent instead, and this stops that one too — it is the same slot at startup, and the reason is the same either way. Per hub it is `adj hub --no-dashboard`, and `adj hub --dashboard` collects once on a machine that has this set to false; the flag becomes ADJUTANT_STARTUP_DASHBOARD on the agent's command line and outranks whatever is written here. Unlike every other setting on this list it is a true/false, not a command: a string "false" is reported in `warnings` and ignored.
defaults.//hubServe: Whether the MCP server started under a hub also serves that hub's board, for as long as the hub runs. Default: true. It takes 127.0.0.1:4577 when that is free and any free port when it is not; the hub reads the URL from `board` in adjutant_config. A board already running for the hub, started by hand with `adj serve`, is left alone. Set it to false to keep the board to `adj serve`, or to open no local port. A true/false, like startupDashboard.
defaults.//julesKey: Command that prints the Jules API key, for `adj jules`. Default: the macOS keychain item jules-api (`security find-generic-password -s jules-api -w`); add it with `security add-generic-password -s jules-api -a "$USER" -w` and type the key at the prompt. A command rather than the key itself, because `adj config` prints every setting and an agent reads it. The key goes to curl on stdin and is taken out of anything printed back. Set it to false to turn handing tasks to Jules off.
defaults.//worktreePattern: Where a worktree goes when no convention tool answers. Default: .claude/worktrees/{name} — the same shape such a tool uses, on purpose: two answers for where a worktree lives is worse than either. Placeholders: {repo} {branch} {name}. **{name} here is the branch with its slashes flattened** (`someone/app-1234` -> `someone-app-1234`), which is not the {name} in a branchPattern — that one is the task's own name (`app-1234`). Two different values with one spelling, so read each pattern's own list. The branch shape has its own fallback ({user}/{name}); override it per task source with that source's branchPattern. A {branch} containing `..` is refused rather than resolved: it would name a path outside the checkout.
defaults.//skills: Named procedures the prompts hand off to, if this machine has them. Omit any of them and the prompts skip that step.

example/android-app.//: One code repo drawing from two Project v2 boards. `issueKeys` maps each issue repo to its key: a board holds issues from several repos, so the key is a property of the issue, not of the source. No branchPattern/worktreeName below — the worktree convention supplies the shape, adjutant passes `{issueKey}-{issue}`, and worktreeName defaults to `{issuekey-lowercase}-{issue}`. Set them per source only for a tracker that has no convention.

issueCreate.//: How the hub files a newly reported bug. Point `command` at the repo's own issue-creation procedure instead of hand-rolling `gh issue create` — templates, labels and board registration live there. Omit the whole key and the hub asks once, then offers to write it here. `notes` carries that procedure's quirks, which the generic prompt cannot know: whether it is interactive, which questions it asks, whether the body can be intercepted before posting, what checks it already runs, and what has to be done afterwards. Repo-wide rules (AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md) do NOT belong here — the hub runs in that repo's checkout and already loads them.
issueCreate.//notes: One line per quirk, in the order the hub will hit them. These are made up; write what your own command actually does.
notes: Interactive: asks for template kind, parent issue, title and detail in one prompt.
Posts without showing a draft first, so the body cannot be intercepted.
Already runs its own secret and personal-data check; do not run one around it.
Does not register the issue on the board — do that afterwards.

projectFields.//: Fixed ids for this board's Status field, so the hub does not look them up on every run. projectId: `gh project view <n> --owner <o> --format json --jq .id`. statusFieldId and the option ids: `gh project field-list <n> --owner <o> --format json`, then read the Status field.

taskSources.//: Seasonal board. Its Status column has no In Progress at all, so projectFields is omitted and the hub only assigns. Issues from example/team-seasonal show up on both boards; the hub dedupes by owner/repo#number.

example/android-app.//agentEnv: Environment the hub and its workers are both started with. For a repo that runs under a separate agent profile: if the hub and its workers land in different config directories, their MCP servers, auth and history disagree. Keys have to be variable names — letters, digits and underscore, not starting with a digit — because these are assembled into an `env K=V …` command line; anything else is dropped and reported in `warnings`. Do not write `~`: which side expands it varies.
example/android-app.//postCreate: Commands run once, in the main checkout, right after a worktree is created — `{worktree}` is its absolute path. This is where gitignored files a build needs (signing certs, local.properties) get carried across, since nothing else copies them.
example/android-app.//verify: What a worker runs to prove its change works before handing over. Written here rather than guessed, because the wrong build command reads as a broken change.
example/android-app.//onWorktreeRemove: Commands run right after a worktree is removed (by the hub or from the board), in the main checkout, with `{worktree}` (full path) and `{name}` (directory name) substituted — for anything living outside it that would otherwise be left behind (a container, a simulator, a registered device).

example/web.//: Plain GitHub Issues in the same repo. Single source, so the flat shorthand: a top-level `taskSource` is read as a `taskSources` of one. issueKeys still lives at the entry level, even with one entry in it.

example/service.//: Linear. `team` is the key prefix, e.g. XYZ-4902.

example/legacy.//: Jira. cloudId comes from the tracker's own resource list.
